title: Consequentialism
text: Consequentialism is the view that morality is all about producing the right kinds of overall consequences. Here the phrase 'overall consequences' of an action means everything the action brings about, including the action itself. Consequentialists say that moral decisions should be based on the overall consequences of our actions, not on the actions themselves. The most famous version of consequentialism is utilitarianism, which holds that the right action is the one that produces the most overall happiness or well-being. Critics argue that consequentialism can justify harming innocent people if it produces better overall consequences. Defenders respond that rule-consequentialism can avoid such counterintuitive results by evaluating rules rather than individual acts.

title: Kant's Moral Philosophy
text: Kant's moral philosophy is organized around the idea of moral duty. Kant argues that the only thing unconditionally good is a good will. A good will is one that acts from duty, not from inclination or self-interest. The moral worth of an action depends on the maxim (principle) behind it, not on its consequences. Kant formulates the Categorical Imperative in several ways. The Universal Law formulation states: 'Act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.' The Humanity formulation states: 'Act in such a way that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never merely as a means to an end, but always at the same time as an end.' Critics argue that Kant's ethics is too rigid and doesn't account for the importance of consequences or emotions in moral decision-making.

title: Virtue Ethics
text: Virtue ethics is currently one of three major approaches in normative ethics. It may, initially, be identified as the one that emphasizes the virtues, or moral character, in contrast to the approach that emphasizes duties or rules (deontology) or that emphasizes the consequences of actions (consequentialism). Suppose it is obvious that someone in need should be helped. A utilitarian will point to the fact that the consequences of doing so will maximize well-being, a deontologist to the fact that, in doing so the agent will be acting in accordance with a moral rule such as 'Do unto others as you would be done by' and a virtue ethicist to the fact that helping the person would be charitable or benevolent. Virtue ethics is not so much interested in the question 'What should I do?' but rather in the question 'What kind of person should I be?' It focuses on the development of character traits (virtues) that enable a person to live a good life.

title: Care Ethics
text: Care ethics is a moral theory that emphasizes the importance of relationships and care in moral decision-making. It was developed largely in response to the perceived limitations of traditional ethical theories like Kantian ethics and utilitarianism, which were seen as overly abstract and detached from the concrete realities of human relationships. Care ethicists argue that moral decisions should be based on the particularities of specific situations and the needs of particular individuals, rather than on universal principles. Key concepts in care ethics include attentiveness, responsibility, competence, and responsiveness. Critics argue that care ethics can lead to favoritism and may not provide sufficient guidance for dealing with strangers or large-scale moral problems.

title: Social Contract Theory
text: Social contract theory, nearly as old as philosophy itself, is the view that persons' moral and/or political obligations are dependent upon a contract or agreement among them to form the society in which they live. Socrates uses something quite like a social contract argument to explain to Crito why he must remain in prison and accept the death penalty. However, social contract theory is rightly associated with modern moral and political theory and is given its first full exposition and defense by Thomas Hobbes. After Hobbes, John Locke and Jean-Jacques Rousseau are the best known proponents of this enormously influential theory, which has been one of the most dominant theories within moral and political theory throughout the history of the modern West. In the twentieth century, moral and political theory regained philosophical momentum as a result of John Rawls' Kantian version of social contract theory, and was followed by new analyses of the subject by David Gauthier and others.

title: Doctrine of Double Effect
text: The doctrine (or principle) of double effect is often invoked to explain the permissibility of an action that causes a serious harm, such as the death of a human being, as a side effect of promoting some good end. It is claimed that sometimes it is permissible to cause such a harm as a side effect (or 'double effect') of bringing about a good result even though it would not be permissible to cause such a harm as a means to bringing about the same good end. The doctrine of double effect is often mentioned in discussions of euthanasia, abortion, and trolley problems. The doctrine was originally proposed by Thomas Aquinas and has been developed by contemporary philosophers including Elizabeth Anscombe and Judith Jarvis Thomson. Critics argue that the distinction between intended and merely foreseen consequences is not morally relevant, or that the doctrine leads to counterintuitive results.
